setupSteps: Remember the rule: more weight on the pin = more help = easier. The number is the help, not the load you lift.

Work out your lifted load: body weight minus the pin number. One guide's example: a 180 lb person using 50 lb of assistance lifts about 130 lb. In kg: a 70 kg person using 30 kg of help lifts about 40 kg (est.). Log that figure, not only the pin number.

Check the units and steps: many machines show kg or lb and step in plate increments that may be 5 lb or 5 kg or other values; read the placard. Increments vary by machine (the size of the step is Not found as a standard). Some machines add small "half" weights; ask staff.

Starting assistance: sources differ. One says about 60% of your body weight if you have never done it; others say enough help for 6–10 (or 8–10) clean, controlled reps; another says 3 sets of 5–8. FitPlate's choice: pick the assistance that allows 8–10 clean reps with 3–4 reps in reserve, which for many first-timers is roughly half to two-thirds of body weight (est., not validated). If you can do more than 12 reps easily, lower the help by one step next time.
Push the pin fully in so it cannot fall out; check the number before you kneel.
Kneel pad: place both knees on the pad, shins flat, torso upright and tall. The pad rises as you pull and sinks as you lower. Let it settle before you begin.
Step platform: stand on the platform with feet flat and use it for balance only; do not push off hard with your legs.

How to get on and off: step or kneel on with the pad at its lowest position, reach up and take the handles, and lower yourself until the arms are straight. At the end, stand up (or step back) and let the pad rise gently before letting go; never drop the last bit.
If your arms cannot reach straight: use a lower pad setting or a machine with a platform that starts lower; ask staff. Some machines have a height adjustment (not all).
Wide overhand (pronated): hands slightly outside shoulder width, thumbs around the handles, wrists straight. Most lat-focused.
Neutral (palms facing): hands about shoulder width on the parallel handles. Many people find it the kindest to the shoulders and elbows; often the best choice for beginners.
Underhand (supinated, chin-up): hands about shoulder width, palms facing you. Uses the biceps most; start with extra assistance and avoid it if elbows or wrists hurt.

No direct source was found comparing neutral and overhand grips specifically on this machine (Not found). One 2017 study of free pull-ups found a towel pull-up gave lower middle-trapezius activity than a traditional pull-up (snippet), so grips change which muscles work.
Switch to the dip handles: the machine has either a separate set of dip handles or a position change. Read the placard; ask staff the first time.
Platform or kneel pad: on many machines you kneel on the pad again, or stand on a platform with your hands on the dip bars at your sides and arms straight, shoulders pressed down away from the ears.

Depth limit: most sources say stop when the upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor, where the elbow bends to about 90 degrees (est.); one coaching blog argues the right depth depends on your shoulder and that parallel is a competition cue, not a universal limit. FitPlate uses about 90 degrees as the limit for beginners.
Torso: a slight forward lean works the chest more; upright works the triceps more (coach-level). Keep it small and steady.

steps.title: Set the pin
steps.action: Choose the assistance (section 3, point 4) and push the pin fully in.
steps.visualCheck: Side: pin in. Front: nothing blocking the handles.

steps.title: Get on the pad or platform
steps.action: Kneel on the pad with shins flat or stand on the platform; take the handles with straight arms.
steps.feel: A gentle hang through the arms and sides of the back.
steps.visualCheck: Side: torso upright, no swing. Front: hands level, wrists straight.

steps.title: Set the shoulder blades
steps.action: Pull the shoulder blades gently down, away from the ears, with arms still straight.
steps.feel: The muscles under the armpits switch on; shoulders away from the ears.

steps.title: Pull the elbows down
steps.action: Drive the elbows down and toward your hips so the chest rises toward the handles.
steps.feel: The back muscles pulling the elbows, not the hands.
steps.visualCheck: Front: elbows pointing down; head stays neutral. Side: torso still.

steps.title: Reach the top
steps.action: Bring the chin level with or just above the handles, chest toward the hands, without craning the neck.
steps.feel: A squeeze between the shoulder blades.
steps.visualCheck: Front: elbows bent about 90 degrees or less (est.); chin not pushed forward.

steps.title: Lower slowly
steps.action: Straighten the arms under control; let the shoulder blades rise last; do not drop.
steps.feel: A controlled stretch in the lats while the pad sinks smoothly.
steps.visualCheck: Side: no bounce; arms end nearly straight.

steps.title: Repeat, then finish
steps.action: Repeat steps 3–6. After the last rep, stand up or step off while still holding the handles and let the pad rise gently.

steps.title: Take the dip position
steps.action: On the dip handles with arms straight, shoulders pressed down, chest slightly up.
steps.feel: Arms supporting you; shoulders away from the ears.
steps.visualCheck: Front: elbows close to the body, wrists straight. Side: small, steady lean.

steps.title: Lower slowly
steps.action: Bend the elbows and lower until the upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor (about 90 degrees at the elbow, est.).
steps.feel: A stretch across the chest and a controlled load in the triceps; no pinching at the front of the shoulder.
steps.visualCheck: Side: elbows not flared, shoulders not rolling forward past the handles.

steps.title: Press back up
steps.action: Push the handles down to straighten the arms, keeping the shoulders down.
steps.feel: Triceps and chest pushing; no shoulder shrug.
steps.visualCheck: Front: arms straight at the top without locking hard.

steps.title: Stop if the front of the shoulder pinches. Reduce depth, add assistance, or switch to the chest press machine (Gym 22) or chair dips (Home 11) with a short range

commonMistakes.title: Choosing too little assistance too early
commonMistakes.text: Choosing too little assistance too early. Why: the rep turns into a heave and the shoulders shrug. Fix: add assistance until you can do 8–10 clean reps.

commonMistakes.title: Choosing too much assistance and riding the pad
commonMistakes.text: Choosing too much assistance and riding the pad. Why: one source warns that max assistance is not challenging enough to build strength. Fix: lower the help one step at a time once you reach the top of your rep range.

commonMistakes.title: Reading the pin as your load
commonMistakes.text: Reading the pin as your load. Why: more weight is more help, so the "heavier" pin is the easier one. Fix: track body weight minus pin.

commonMistakes.title: Swinging or kicking
commonMistakes.text: Swinging or kicking. Why: momentum replaces muscle and can strain the shoulders. Fix: brace the trunk, keep the knees on the pad and slow the tempo.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping on the lowering phase
commonMistakes.text: Dropping on the lowering phase. Why: you lose the most useful part of the rep and can jolt the shoulders. Fix: 3 seconds down.

commonMistakes.title: Pushing off the platform with the legs
commonMistakes.text: Pushing off the platform with the legs. Why: the legs do the work. Fix: use the platform for balance only (as one guide says).

commonMistakes.title: Shrugging and craning the neck to reach the top
commonMistakes.text: Shrugging and craning the neck to reach the top. Why: the upper trapezius takes over and the neck tightens. Fix: shoulders down first; chin level; stop a little lower rather than craning.

commonMistakes.title: Going too deep in dips with flared elbows
commonMistakes.text: Going too deep in dips with flared elbows. Why: the front of the shoulder takes extra stress; the evidence is limited (see section 9), but pinching is a warning. Fix: stop at about 90 degrees at the elbow and keep the elbows close.

commonMistakes.title: Stepping off and letting the pad crash up
commonMistakes.text: Stepping off and letting the pad crash up. Why: noise and a hazard for neighbours. Fix: stand up holding the handles and let the pad rise gently.

commonMistakes.title: Skipping mode checks
commonMistakes.text: Skipping mode checks. Why: dip handles and pull-up handles use different positions and pads. Fix: read the placard; ask staff.

safetyNotes: Shoulder problems: the fixed path can aggravate a painful shoulder (one retailer blog); dip mode is the main concern. A peer-reviewed review says evidence that dips injure the shoulder is limited (two case reports of pectoralis major rupture, anecdotes), and a 2022 study of dips to exhaustion in healthy men says injury claims have minimal support (snippets); still, avoid dips with current shoulder pain, impingement or instability, and use short range.
High blood pressure: avoid breath-holding; breathe out on the effort; moderate effort.
Lower back pain: no swinging or kicking; keep the trunk braced; use a lat pulldown or seated row if it hurts.
Pregnancy, recent surgery, osteoporosis, heart disease: see the table; ask a professional.

Note: all sources for this item were seen only as search-result summaries (pages not opened in full); nearly all are retailer or coaching blogs and exercise libraries, so the evidence base is weak. The 150/90 degree elbow thresholds, 70 degree dip depth floor, 30 degree swing limit, starting-assistance rule of thumb, and the sets, reps and rest values are FitPlate choices (est.), not validated. Not found: an ACE, NASM, NSCA or ExRx page for this machine; a direct EMG study of machine-assisted versus bodyweight pull-ups or of neutral versus overhand grips on the machine; a standard assistance increment size; a validated beginner starting-assistance norm; and condition-specific sources for knee pain, lower back pain, obesity and PCOS.
